newsitem.title: UK: Grobbelaar walks free in match-fixing trial.
newsitem.headline: Grobbelaar walks free in match-fixing trial.

text.p: Zimbabwean goalkeeper Bruce Grobbelaar walked free from a British court on Friday after a soccer match-fixing trial failed to reach a verdict on a last charge against him.
"It has been hell," the former Liverpool and Southampton star said as he vowed to get back to playing football again.

The 11-strong jury in the trial at Winchester, southern England, reported to Judge Charles McCullough that it had been unable to agree even a 10-1 majority verdict on a charge that the goalkeeping star accepted 2,000 pounds ($3,200) to influence the outcome of games.
A few minutes later, a visibly relieved Grobbelaar emerged from the court to thank everyone who had supported him since allegations against him surfaced.
"For 2-1/2 years I have been living under the constant scrutiny from you media people," he told journalists. "My wife and family have found it hard, very hard, to adjust."
Two other soccer stars, former Aston Villa striker John Fashanu and Dutch-born goalkeeper Hans Segers, were cleared in unanimous verdicts on Thursday.
Malaysian businessman Heng Suan Lim was also unanimously found not guilty.
Grobbelaar, one of the most flamboyant and eccenrtic players in the game, said: "I am sitting here as a free man. It's been finally laid to rest."
He said he had one goal now in his sporting life -- "That is to get Zimbabwe through to the World Cup."

"The verdicts of today and yesterday are a victory for football because it cuts out right from the beginning what we have always said: There's never been a game thrown, never in the future, never in the past."
Grobbelaar's lawyer made no application to the court for the state to pay his legal costs after applications on behalf of Fashanu and Segers were rejected on Thursday.
The freed defendants returned to the court on Friday, taking their seats in the public gallery.
It was the second time the four defendants had faced trial for the same offences. Another jury was dismissed earlier this year after failing to reach verdicts.
The four had all denied the allegations that they were involved with an Asian gambling syndicate.

The prosecution had investigated huge cash sums the defendants deposited in their bank accounts and traced dozens of telephone calls they made to one another, but the jury concluded these were not proof they had been rigging matches.
The case is reported to have cost millions of pounds and has dented the image of English football.
The English Football Association announced after Thursday's ruling that it was carrying out a detailed inquiry into the rules on betting and forecasting in the game.
The former deputy Commissioner of London's Metropolitan Police Sir John Smith is leading the inquiry and is due to report back within three months.
